items.title: Medical Physics: Introduction and Radiations Used

source_refs.note: Chapter opening and the introduction to radiations (PDF 156-157). The learning outcomes are not reproduced.

blocks.text: Medical physics is the branch of physics that applies physical principles and techniques to medicine, especially to the diagnosis and treatment of disease. It combines physics with medical science to develop and use technologies that let doctors see inside the human body and treat patients safely and effectively. It improves the accuracy of medical imaging, reduces radiation risks and enhances treatment. In hospitals and diagnostic centres it is used in X-ray imaging, ultrasound, CT scans and PET scans, which let doctors detect fractures, diagnose tumours and study internal organs without surgery. This chapter covers the piezoelectric effect and ultrasound, the production and use of X-rays, CT scanning and PET.

Radiation is the transfer of energy through space or matter as waves or particles. In medical physics it is used mainly for diagnosis (imaging) and treatment. It is classified as ionising or non-ionising. Ionising radiation has enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, producing ions; non-ionising radiation does not. Examples of ionising radiation used in medicine are X-rays, gamma rays and positrons (from radioactive tracers); X-rays and gamma rays interact with matter through the photoelectric effect and Compton scattering. Examples of non-ionising radiation are ultrasound waves and radio waves, which are reflected, refracted or absorbed when they meet matter.

X-rays are commonly used to image bones and internal organs; gamma rays are used in nuclear medicine, such as PET scans, and in cancer treatment because of their high penetrating power. Ultrasound is used to examine soft tissues, monitor the fetus and study internal organs safely without ionising radiation. Radio waves are used in MRI, where they interact with atomic nuclei to produce detailed images of soft tissues without harmful radiation exposure.

blocks.prompt: Classify X-rays, ultrasound, gamma rays and radio waves as ionising or non-ionising.
blocks.explanation: Ionising: X-rays and gamma rays. Non-ionising: ultrasound and radio waves.

items: Medical physics applies physics to diagnosis and treatment.
Ionising (X-rays, gamma rays, positrons) can remove electrons; non-ionising (ultrasound, radio waves) cannot.
